Kings, Books of First and Second

body.p: KAB*
According to Josephus, a dry measure equaling about a quart. Other authorities think the kab was larger (see 2 Kgs 6:25, nasb mg). See Weights and Measures.
KABZEEL

City located in the extreme south of Yehudah’s/Judah’s territory adjacent to neighboring Edom (Jos 15:21; also called Yekavtse’el/Jekabzeel in Neh 11:25). Benayah/Benaiah, one of David’s valiant warriors, came from there (2 Sm 23:20; 1 Chr 11:22). The reference in Nehemyah/Nehemiah indicates that Yehudah’s tribe returned to this area after the exile. Its exact site is not known, but Khirbet Hora has been suggested.
KADESH, KADESH-BARNEA

Home of the wandering Israelis/Israelites for nearly 38 years. In the vast area of the Sinay/Sinai there are two main oases: in the south is Wadi Feiran, near the mountain of Mosheh/Moses (Mt Sinay or Horev/Horeb); in the north is Kadesh, or Kadesh-Barnea/Kadesh-barnea. The former was the place where the law was given; the latter, the main campsite of the 12 tribes during their exodus from Mitsrayim/Egypt (Dt 1:46).

Kadesh-Barnea (Gn 14:7, “Eyn-Mishpat/En-mishpat”) was raided by Kedorla’omer/Chedorlaomer, king of Eylam/Elam, during the time of Avraham/Abraham. In this area Hagar was driven from the tent of Sarah, her mistress (16:14), and here Miryam/Miriam died and was buried (Nm 20:1). The great contention over water took place here, giving rise to the name Merivah/Meribah or Meribath-kadesh (Nm 20:2-24; Dt 32:51; Ez 47:19; 48:28). This was also the scene of Korah’s rebellion against the leadership of Mosheh and Aharon/Aaron (Nm 16–17). This area would long remain in the memory of the Israeli/Israelite tribes as the place of their unbelief following the report of the 10 spies and a delay of 38 years before their occupancy of the Promised Land (Ps 95:8-11; cf. Heb 3:7-19).

Because of the water, pasture, and agricultural lands, plus its proximity to Kena’an/Canaan, the Israelis found this area the best spot in which to spend most of their time prior to entering the Promised Land.
See also Meribah #2; Wilderness Wanderings.
KADMIEL

Head of a Levite family who returned from the exile with Zerubavel/Zerubbabel (Ezr 2:40; Neh 7:43; 12:8). His name appears in the list of those who supervised the temple rebuilding project (Ezr 3:9), participated in sealing the covenant (Neh 10:9), and were prominent in the praise service (9:4-5; 12:24).
KADMONITES

Semitic tribe whose land was promised to Avraham’s/Abraham’s descendants (Gn 15:19). The name of the tribe is the same as the Hebrew adjective “eastern” and suggests that references to peoples or lands of the east (Gn 25:6; Jgs 8:10; 1 Kgs 4:30; Jb 1:3) may be synonymous with the tribal name.
KAIN (Place)

Town in the Yehudi/Jew hill country (Jos 15:57). Its place in the same district as the known cities of Maeon/Maon, Karmel/Carmel, Zif/Ziph, and Yutah/Juttah (v 55) favors its identification with Khirbet Yuqim, southwest of Hevron/Hebron.
KAIN* (Tribe)

Clan name synonymous with the Keynim/Kenites (Nm 24:22; Jgs 4:11). The name is Hebrew for “spear,” suggesting a tribe of metalworkers. The nomadic tribe was friendly (1 Sm 15:6) and was eventually absorbed by Yehudah/Judah. See Kenites.
KAIWAN
Mesopotamian astral deity, called “Chiun” in the kjv and “Kiyun/Kiyyun” in the nasb (Am 5:26). See Sakkuth.
KALLAI
Priest and the head of Salu’s/Sallu’s (Salu’s) priestly family during the days of Yoyakim/Joiakim the high priest (Neh 12:20).
KAMON

City in Gilead where Yair/Jair the judge was buried (Jgs 10:5). While the place has not been identified with certainty, modern Kameim, a small village southeast of the Sea of Galil/Galilee, probably reflects the original name, if not the exact location.
KANAH

1. Brook forming Efrayim’s/Ephraim’s northern border and the southern border of Menasheh’s/Manasseh’s tribe (Jos 16:8; 17:9). It flowed westward, joining the Yarkon River about five miles (8 kilometers) from the Mediterranean just north of the modern city of Tel Aviv (biblical Yafo/Joppa). It is dry most of the year. Kanah is today called Wadi Qana.

2. City situated along Asher’s border (Jos 19:28). It lay about six miles (9.7 kilometers) southeast of Tsor/Tyre on one of the major northeast-southwest routes through northern Galil/Galilee. Qana (in modern Levanon/Lebanon) still bears the name and marks the site.
KANATHA*

One of the original 10 Greek cities rebuilt by Romai/Rome after Pompey’s conquest of Palestine and Aram/Syria around 63 BC. The region of these cities became known as the Dekapolis/Decapolis. Kanatha (also spelled Canatha), positioned about 60 miles (96.5 kilometers) east of the Sea of Galil/Galilee, formed the easternmost boundary of the Dekapolis. Some suggest that the city is identifiable with Kenat/Kenath of Numbers 32:42 and the subsequent modern town of Qanawat, a short distance northeast of es-Suweideh in the Havran/Hauran region.
See also Decapolis; Kenath.
KAREAH

Father of Yonatan/Jonathan and Yohanan/Johanan (2 Kgs 25:23). After Yerushalem/Jerusalem fell to Nevukadnetsar’s/Nebuchadnezzar’s army, his sons joined Gedalyah/Gedaliah at Mitspah/Mizpah (Jer 40:8–43:5).
KARKA

Unidentified town marking a part of Yehudah’s/Judah’s southern boundary (Jos 15:3). It was located in the southwest section of Palestine between Kadesh-Barnea/Kadesh-barnea and Wadi el-Arish (Besor Brook).
KARKOR

City in the Transjordan where Gid’on/Gideon attacked the armies of the two Midyanite/Midianite kings, Zevah/Zebah and Tsalmuna/Zalmunna (Jgs 8:10). Indications of its location are sketchy. Judges 8:11 places it east of Novah/Nobah and Jog-behah, a town identified with Jubeiah, which is seven miles (11.3 kilometers) northwest of Amman in Yarden/Jordan. A more feasible site is in the vicinity of ancient Sukot/Succoth (Tell Dier ‘Alla) and Penuel (Tell edh-Dhahab esh-Sherqiyeh), both assigned to Gad’s tribe in Gilead.
KARNAIM

Town situated along the King’s Highway and along one of the northeastern tributaries of the Yarmuk River, 22 miles (35.4 kilometers) east of the Sea of Galil/Galilee on the Transjordan Plateau. The prophet Amos prophesied against Karnayim/Karnaim (also spelled Karnayim), foretelling its impending destruction on account of its wickedness (Am 6:13).

It was the leading town in the area after the decline of its sister city, Ashtarot/Ashtaroth, and became the main center of an Assyrian province in the seventh century BC. In 163 BC it was captured by Yehudah/Judas Maccabeus (1 Macc 5:26, 43-44). Christian and Jewish traditions believe it to be the home of Iyov/Job.
See also Ashteroth-karnaim.
KARTAH

Levitical city in Zevulun’s/Zebulun’s territory. The list of cities assigned to the Merari/Merarite clan of Levites in Joshua 21:34 mentions Kartah, but the parallel passage in 1 Chronicles 6:77 (in the Hebrew) does not.
KARTAN
Levitical town assigned to the Gershonim/Gershonites from the tribe of Naftali/Naphtali (Jos 21:32). It is called Kiryatayim/Kiriathaim in 1 Chronicles 6:76. See Kiriathaim #2; Levitical Cities.
KATTATH
Town assigned to Zevulun/Zebulun (Jos 19:15), perhaps the same as the Kitron of Judges 1:30. See Kitron.
KEBAR

Canal in Bavel/Babylonia. The prophet Yehezkel/Ezekiel, who was among the exiles from the southern kingdom of Yehudah/Judah, received visions from God while living in the area of the Kevar/Kebar Canal (Ez 1:1, 3; 3:15, 23; 10:15, 20, 22; 43:3). Secular Babylonian texts refer to a nar Kabaru that is believed to be the same canal.
KEDAR
1. Second son of Yishmael/Ishmael, Avraham’s/Abraham’s son (Gn 25:13; 1 Chr 1:29).

2. Tribe or area appearing mainly in the prophetic writings from Shelomoh/Solomon to the exile. In Yeshayah’s/Isaiah’s prophecy against Arav/Arabia, Kedar is mentioned twice (Is 21:13-17). Along with Arav, Dedan, and Teyma/Tema, the Kedarites are threatened with destruction. The pomp attributed to them in verse 16 indicates some degree of affluence (see also Ez 27:21), and the militaristic tone of verse 17 points to the fact that they were a warring people. In Jeremiah 49:28 Kedar is linked with Hatsor/Hazor as victims of Nevukadnetsar’s/Nebuchadnezzar’s conquests. Although there is no extrabiblical record of Nevukadnetsar’s march on Kedar, Ashurbanipal, the king of Ashur/Assyria, does mention the conquest of Kedar. That would have been about 650 BC, or a half a century earlier than the Babylonian conquest. Apart from Ashurbanipal’s account, the only other ancient extrabiblical reference to Kedar is found on a silver bowl offered to the Aravi/Arabian goddess Han-’ilat in the Mitsri/Egyptian Delta. The inscription on the bowl reads, “Kayin/Cain, son of Geshem, king of Kedar,” and the date is firmly fixed in the fifth century BC. This Geshem was very likely the enemy of Nehemyah/Nehemiah (Neh 2:19; 6:1-6).

The picture the Bible gives of Kedar is that of a desert nomadic people descended from Yishmael. They were not initially believers in Yahweh but are included in Yeshayah’s prophecy of the future kingdom of God (cf. Is 42:11; 60:7). Their desert environment limited their work to sheep herding and trading. Because of unpredictable water supplies in the desert, they were constantly moving—a way of life best handled by living in tents rather than permanent houses (cf. Ps 120:5; Sg 1:5). For this reason archaeologists have found no site named Kedar. All we can surmise is that the area of Kedar lay to the east and slightly to the south of Yisrael/Israel in what is today the southern part of Yarden/Jordan. The people of Kedar presumably died out or were assimilated into the surrounding nations.
KEDEMAH
Son of Yishmael/Ishmael (Gn 25:15) who gave his name to the tribe he fathered (1 Chr 1:31).
KEDEMOTH

City east of the Yarden/Jordan, probably located on the upper course of the Arnon River. From the wilderness of Kedemot/Kedemoth, Mosheh/Moses sent messengers to Sihon, king of Heshbon, asking permission to pass peaceably through his land (Dt 2:26). In the division of the land, Kedemot was given to Re’uven’s/Reuben’s tribe (Jos 13:18) and then set aside as one of the Levitical cities for the Merarim/Merarites (Jos 21:37; 1 Chr 6:79).
See also Levitical Cities.
KEDESH
1. Town in the Yehudi/Jew Negev (Jos 15:23); its appearance alongside Ad’adah/Adadah (Aroer) argues against its identification with Kadesh-Barnea/Kadesh-barnea.

2. City of refuge in upper Galil/Galilee, in the territory of Naftali/Naphtali (Jos 20:7), set apart for the Gershoni/Gershonite clan of Levi (Jos 21:32; 1 Chr 6:76), and the home of Barak (Jgs 4:6). It was conquered by Tiglat-Pileser/Tiglath-pileser III in 732 BC (2 Kgs 15:29). Yonatan/Jonathan Maccabeus defeated the army of Demetrios/Demetrius there (1 Macc 11:63, 73). It is identified with Tell Qades, four and a half miles (7.2 kilometers) northwest of Lake Huleh.
See also Cities of Refuge.
3. Levitical city in Yisakar/Issachar (1 Chr 6:72); the parallel passage has Kishyon/Kishion (Jos 21:28).
See also Levitical Cities.
KEDORLAOMER

King of Eylam/Elam who participated with three other kings in a campaign against five cities near the southern end of the Dead Sea plain (Gn 14). Although Kedorlaomer is initially third in the list (v 1), he was evidently the leader of the four kings. Elsewhere in the chapter his name comes first or stands alone.

For 12 years the five cities of the plain were vassals of Kedorlaomer. In the 13th year the cities rebelled, and the next year Kedorlaomer enlisted allies to enforce his lordship. The victorious kings looted the cities and took prisoners. Because the patriarch Avram’s/Abram’s nephew Lot was among the captives, Avram mustered his servants and allies and pursued Kedorlaomer as far as Damesek/Damascus. Kedorlaomer was defeated, and the captured loot and prisoners were rescued.

The first half of the name Kedorlaomer is a common Eylami/Elamite word meaning “servant.” The second half is probably the name of an Eylami deity. Although both elements of the name are known outside the Bible, the combination is not. It fits, however, with an early second-millennium BC date for the encounter, coinciding with the biblical account.
KEHELATHAH
One of the places where the Israelis/Israelites encamped on their journey from Mitsrayim/Egypt to Mt Sinay/Sinai, located somewhere between Risah/Rissah and Mt Shepher (Nm 33:22-23).
KEILAH (Person)
Kalev’s/Caleb’s descendant from Yehudah’s/Judah’s tribe, called the Garmi/Garmite in 1 Chronicles 4:19. Some identify this reference with the city in Yehudah instead of a person.
KEILAH (Place)

City assigned to Yehudah’s/Judah’s tribe (Jos 15:44; 1 Chr 4:19), located in the southeast Shefelah/Shephelah near the Pelishti/Philistine border. It is identified with modern Khirbet Qila, eight and a half miles (13.7 kilometers) northwest of Hevron/Hebron.

David led a daring expedition to Ke’ilah/Keilah to deliver it from marauding Pelishti bands, who were stealing grain from its threshing floors. He made it his residence for a time and expected to gain the loyalty of its people. However, when it became evident that the men of Ke’ilah were plotting to turn him and his men over to Sha’ul/Saul, he retreated into the wilderness of Zif/Ziph (1 Sm 23:1-14).

Ke’ilah was reinhabited by Yehudim/Jews after the Captivity and was divided into two districts, ruled by Hashavyah/Hashabiah and Bavay/Bavvai. Its rulers were included in the roster of those who participated in rebuilding the Yerushalem/Jerusalem wall under Nehemyah/Nehemiah (Neh 3:17-18).
KELAIAH

A Levite who was guilty of marrying a pagan wife (Ezr 10:18). According to verse 23 Kelayah/Kelaiah is also called Kelita. A Levite named Kelita is also found in Nehemiah 8:7, 10:10, and 1 Esdras 9:48, where he is one who helped Ezra in expounding the law and who set his seal on Ezra’s covenant. It cannot be determined with certainty whether Kelayah and Kelita are the same individual.
KELAL
See Chelal.
KELITA
A Levite sometimes thought to be the same as Kelayah/Kelaiah. See Kelaiah.
KELUB
See Chelub.
KELUBAI*
See Chelubai.
KELUHI
One of Bani’s sons, who was encouraged by Ezra to divorce his foreign wife after the exile (Ezr 10:35).
KEMUEL
1. Third son of Nahor (Avraham’s/Abraham’s brother) and the father of Aram (Gn 22:21).
2. Shiftan’s/Shiphtan’s son from Efrayim’s/Ephraim’s tribe; one of 12 men appointed to divide the land among the Israeli/Israelite tribes (Nm 34:24).
3. Hashavyah’s/Hashabiah’s father, a ruler of the Levites during David’s reign (1 Chr 27:17).
KENAANAH
1. Father of Tsidkiyah/Zedekiah, the false prophet who incorrectly prophesied victory for kings Ahav/Ahab and Yehoshafat/Jehoshaphat over the Aramim/Syrians (1 Kgs 22:11, 24; 2 Chr 18:10, 23).
2. Bilhan’s son, who was chief of the subclan of Yedieael/Jediael in Benyamin’s/Benjamin’s tribe in the time of King David (1 Chr 7:10-11).
KENAN
Fourth-generation descendant of Adam (Gn 5:9-14; 1 Chr 1:2); alternately called Keynan/Cainan in Lukas’s/Luke’s genealogy of Christ (Lk 3:37, rsv). See Genealogy of Jesus Christ.
KENANI
Levite who participated in Ezra’s public reading of the law after the exile (Neh 9:4).
KENANIAH
1. Levite chief who led processional singing when King David brought the ark of the covenant to the new tabernacle in Yerushalem/Jerusalem (1 Chr 15:1-3, 22, 27).
2. Public administrator during David’s reign. His sons also served as public officials (1 Chr 26:29).
KENATH

Town in the Havran/Hauran taken by Novah/Nobah (Nm 32:42) but later lost to Geshur and Aram (1 Chr 2:23). It was a Kena’ani/Canaanite city known from Mitsri/Egyptian execration texts of the 19th and 18th centuries BC and from the conquest by Thutmose III and the Amarna letters. In the Hellenistic period it became one of the cities of the Dekapolis/Decapolis; Jewish returnees from Bavel/Babylon had settled there, and the rabbis considered it a border town of the Promised Land. It was also called Kanatha.
See also Kanatha.
KENAZ

Singular form of the name of the Kenizi/Kenizzite tribe, whose land was promised to Avraham’s/Abraham’s descendants (Gn 15:19). The appearance of three men by this name in the OT may be explained by the spread of the Kenizi tribe over Edom and southern Yehudah/Judah before the Israeli/Israelite conquest.
1. Grandson of Esav/Esau and chieftain of Edom (Gn 36:11, 15, 42; 1 Chr 1:36, 53).
2. Father of Otniel/Othniel (Jos 15:17; Jgs 1:13; 3:9-11) and Serayah/Seraiah (1 Chr 4:13).
3. Kalev’s/Caleb’s descendant (1 Chr 4:15). See Kenizzites.
KENEZITE*
KJV spelling of Kenizi/Kenizzite in Numbers 32:12 and Joshua 14:6, 14. See Kenizzites.
KENITES

One of 10 tribes living in Kena’an/Canaan during Avraham’s/Abraham’s time (Gn 15:19). The Keynim/Kenites, however, are not included in the parallel statement from Mosheh’s/Moses’ day (Ex 3:17). The apparent reason for this is a more favorable relationship with Yisrael/Israel by that time. That Yisrael continued to accord special treatment to the Keynim is clear from 1 Samuel 15:6. When Sha’ul/Saul mobilized his army against the Amalekim/Amalekites, he gave a warning before the attack. This kindness seems to reflect the aid given by Hovav/Hobab, son of Re’uel/Reuel, who was their guide in the wilderness (Nm 10:29-31).

By the time of Barak the judge and Deborah the prophetess, there was a branch of the Keynim in Galil/Galilee. Judges 4:11 says, “Now Hever/Heber the Keyni/Kenite, a descendant of Mosheh’s brother-in-law Hovav, had moved away from the other members of his tribe and pitched his tent by the Oak of Tsa’ananim/Zaanannim, near Kedesh” (nlt). This Kedesh was in Galil and was not the Kadesh-Barnea/Kadesh-barnea of the Sinay/Sinai wilderness.

Since the name Keyni is closely related to the word for (copper) smith in both Arabic and Aramaic, it may be that this tribe was something of a trade guild of wandering smiths who offered their skills where needed. Nomadic tribes of metalworkers were known to have moved about in the ancient Near East from the early second millennium BC. Such artisans are found among the party of Asiatics pictured on the Beni-Hasan tomb in Mitsrayim/Egypt, dating from the 19th century BC. In modern times at least one Aravi/Arab tribe of gypsylike traveling smiths or tinkers has followed the trade routes in search of employment.

In light of the biblical information about the Keynim, the major question is the influence this seemingly ubiquitous tribe had on the life and culture of the Hebrews. The least likely suggestion is that Mosheh was dependent on his Keyni/Midyanite/Midianite father-in-law, Yitro/Jethro, for making the bronze serpent (Nm 21:4-9). However, it is likely that the Keynim, if indeed expert in metallurgy, may have taught this technology to God’s covenant people to help them achieve settled nationhood. More serious is the suggestion that Yitro (also called Re’uel), “priest of Midyan/Midian,” was the source of Mosheh’s theology—the monotheistic religion of Jehovah (or Yahweh). This suggestion can be countered from two angles—one biblical and the other historical.

The biblical reference specifically stating that Jehovah was the personal God known to godly men from the earliest generations is Genesis 4:26: “And to Shet/Seth, to him also there was born a son; and he called his name Enosh. Then began men to call upon the name of Jehovah” (asv). Equally significant is the fact that Mosheh’s mother (or ancestress, as some would conclude) bore the name Yokeved/Jochebed, “Jehovah is glory.” Obviously, then, Mosheh did not first hear of Jehovah from his father-in-law during his exile in the wilderness of Midyan. The historical evidence indicates that no cultic sites (worship centers) other than the mobile tabernacle were located in Sinay or anywhere south of Be’er-Sheva/Beersheba. It was south of that city that the God who earlier revealed himself to the patriarchs at various localities in the north announced to Mosheh that he was none other than the God of Avraham, of Yitshak/Isaac, and of Ya’akov/Jacob (Ex 3:6). The Israelis/Israelites never returned to Sinay for worship, even though God had first revealed himself to them there.

Yitro clearly learned of Jehovah through Mosheh, not vice versa. Those Keynim who became part of the family of God’s people did so by adoption, by introduction through Yisrael’s witness into the covenant relationship with the God of Ya’akov.

Interestingly, 1 Chronicles 2:55 includes the Keyni Hamat/Hammath, father of the Recabites, within the genealogy of Yehudah’s/Judah’s tribe, into which they had been assimilated. David also links the Keynim with other inhabitants of southern Yehudah (1 Sm 27:10). Jeremiah 35 states that the Recabites preserved the simple nomadic life of their ancestors down to the time of the Babylonian captivity. This, too, conforms to what is known about the nature of the Keynim.
KENIZZITES

A people related to Kenaz, grandson of Esav/Esau (Gn 36:11, 15). The Kenizim/Kenizzites were of Edomi/Edomite stock and resided to the southeast of Yehudah/Judah in the vicinity of the Keynim/Kenites. They are thought to belong to the pre-Israelite population of Kena’an/Canaan (Gn 15:19). Their territory was to be given to the Israelis/Israelites along with that of the Keynim, the Amorim/Amorites, and the Kena’anim/Canaanites (vv 19-21).

In Numbers and Yehoshua/Joshua, Kalev/Caleb, the faithful spy, is reckoned to belong to the Kenizim (Nm 32:12; Jos 14:6, 14). According to 1 Chronicles 4:15, Kalev’s genealogy is traced back to Yehudah (1 Chr 4:1). The relationship of Kalev to the Kenizim is far from clear. Kalev established his patrimony at Kiryat-Sefer/Kiriath-sepher (Jgs 1:11-13), which is in Yehudah but which is also situated close to the territory of the Kenizim. Critical opinion views the Kenizim as non-Israelites who occupied Hevron/Hebron, Devir/Debir, and the southernmost hill country of the Negev and became politically incorporated into Yehudah.
KEPHAR-AMMONI
City allotted to Benyamin’s/Benjamin’s tribe for an inheritance after the initial conquest of Kena’an/Canaan by Yehoshua/Joshua (Jos 18:24).
KEPHIRAH

Hivi/Hivite city included in a treaty with Yehoshua/Joshua that the Givonim/Gibeonites secured by deception (Jos 9:17). When the Israelis/Israelites conquered the land of Kena’an/Canaan, Kefirah/Kephirah became the property of Benyamin’s/Benjamin’s tribe (18:26). Many inhabitants of this city came back to Judea with the repatriates after the exile (Ezr 2:25; Neh 7:29). The site is now identified as Khirbet Kefireh, located southwest of ancient Giveon/Gibeon.
KERAN
Dishon’s son, a member of the Hori/Horite tribe during Esav’s/Esau’s time (Gn 36:26; 1 Chr 1:41).
KEREN-HAPPUCH
Iyov’s/Job’s third daughter and the sister of Yemimah/Jemimah and Ketsiah/Keziah. She was listed as a member of Iyov’s family at the time of his restoration (Jb 42:14).
KERETHITES

Members of a tribal group that lived in southern Yehudah/Judah near Hevron/Hebron (1 Sm 30:14), mentioned along with the Peletim/Pelethites (2 Sm 8:18). The Kereti/Kerethites were associated with the Pelishtim/Philistines, according to Ezekiel 25:15-17 (cf. Zep 2:5). They were judged with “the rest of the seacoast” for the Pelishtim’s offense against Yisrael/Israel. Since the Pelishtim most likely originated in the islands of the Mediterranean, including Kraitai/Crete, the word Kerethite probably means Kretes/Cretan. “Peleti/Pelethite” is probably an alternate spelling of Pelishti/Philistine.

Because of the Kereti’ Pelishti connections, what is known about the Pelishtim may shed light on them. Archaeological evidence from Kretes murals and Mitsri/Egyptian tomb paintings and temple reliefs shows Pelishtim wearing plumed headdresses. Similarities between Pelishti, Kretes, and Greek pottery designs also suggest a strong link among these Mediterranean peoples.

Kereti and Peletim were hired by David as mercenaries, forming an elite corps of foreign soldiers faithful to him through all his troubles (2 Sm 15:18; 20:7, 23; 1 Kgs 1:38). Later kings may have continued to use them as soldiers, as suggested by the mention of “Karim/Carites” (Kereti?) in 2 Kings 11:4, 19.
KERIOTH

1. Town in the Negev of Yehudah/Judah (Jos 15:25), called Keriyot-Hetsron/Kerioth-hezron. The Hebrew text understands Keriyot/Kerioth and Hetsron/Hezron to be separate towns, the latter being identical to Hatsor/Hazor (v 23).

2. Town in Moav/Moab (Jer 48:24, 41; Am 2:2). From the Moavi/Moabite Stone, it can be located in the southwest tableland of Moav opposite Atarot/Ataroth. It is not counted among the towns of Re’uven/Reuben and Gad (Nm 34: Jos 13); in other lists it is absent while Ar is mentioned (Is 15–16), which leads scholars to equate Ar with Keriyot.
KERIOTH-HEZRON
Town mentioned in Joshua 15:25. See Kerioth #1.
KERITH, The Brook

Also rendered the “Kerith Ravine” (niv), it was the place where the Lord told the prophet Eliyah/Elijah to hide from King Ahav/Ahab during a famine Eliyah had predicted. There he had sufficient water to drink and was fed by ravens each morning and evening (1 Kgs 17:2-6). The brook, or gorge, has traditionally been identified as the Wadi Qelt, west of the Yarden/Jordan River near Yeriho/Jericho. More likely Kerith, indicated in Scripture as “east of the Yarden River,” was located in Gilead, Eliyah’s homeland (v 3).
KEROS
One of the temple servants whose descendants returned to Yerushalem/Jerusalem with Zerubavel/Zerubbabel (Ezr 2:44; Neh 7:47).
KERUB
One of five Babylonian cities from which Israelis/Israelites who could not trace their ancestry returned after the exile (Ezr 2:59; Neh 7:61).
KERYGMA*

Basic evangelistic message proclaimed by the earliest Christians. More fully, it is the proclamation of the death, resurrection, and exaltation of Yeshua/Jesus that leads to an evaluation of his person as both Lord and Christ, confronts one with the necessity of repentance, and promises the forgiveness of sins. The kerygma is drawn from two sources: (1) the fragments of pre-Pauline tradition that lie embedded in the writings of the apostle, and (2) the early evangelistic speeches of Kefa/Peter in the book of Acts. When these two sources are compared, a single basic message emerges.

The kerygma is essentially the same as the gospel, although the term itself emphasizes the manner of delivery somewhat more than the message that is being proclaimed. In the ancient world the king made known his decrees by means of a kerux (a town crier or herald). This person, who often served as a close confidant of the king, would travel throughout the realm announcing to the people whatever the king wished to make known. It is this note of authoritative declaration that is so appropriately transferred to the evangelizing activities of the primitive church.

The simplest outline of the kerygma is made up of (1) a proclamation of the death, resurrection, and exaltation of Yeshua, seen as the fulfillment of prophecy and involving human responsibility; (2) the resultant evaluation of Yeshua as both Lord and Christ; and (3) a summons to repent and receive forgiveness of sins. However, on the basis of a careful study of the actual texts themselves, the kerygma did not contain (1) a declaration of the dawn of the messianic age; (2) any reference to the life and ministry of Yeshua (in contrast to his death and resurrection); or (3) a major emphasis on the Second Coming as part of the evangelistic proclamation. While all of these issues are part of the larger theological presentation of the NT, they do not appear to have been included in the essential apostolic gospel. In any case, they are missing from the various texts that provide the source for the kerygma.

It is evident that the resurrection plays the central role in the drama of redemption. The kerygma always focuses on the resurrection. This supernatural act of God in history authenticates the words and works of Yeshua and constitutes the basis for the Christian hope of immortality. Without the resurrection, the church would be no more than a group of well-intentioned religious people who had placed their faith in the superior philosophical and ethical teachings of an unusually fine man. The resurrection is proof positive that Yeshua is who he said he was. Only if he is the Son of God can his death provide an appropriate and sufficient sacrifice for human sin. Essentially, the kerygma is a declaration that Christ is risen from the dead and that by that great act God has brought salvation.

The kerygma is not a dull recital of historical facts but a dynamic confrontation between the Holy Spirit and the sinful heart of man at the point of its basic need. Who can deny that the reality of the resurrection validates the claims of Christ? Who can resist the compelling logic of the resurrection as it leads irresistibly to the conclusion that Yeshua of Nazaret/Nazareth is the living Lord? To repent and believe is to enter the kingdom of God. The kerygma has as its ultimate goal not a sophisticated theology but a transformed life. It is the declaration that in Christ the new order of eternal life has already entered into time and history.

Many ancient peoples believed that heaven and hell were closed by gates to which certain deities and angelic beings had keys. In Greek mythology, for example, Pluto kept the key to hades. Jewish writings near the time of Yeshua give God the key to the abode of the dead. In the book of Revelation, Yohan/John sees Christ holding the keys of death and hades (Rv 1:18; see 3:7).

In Matay’s/Matthew’s Gospel the keys symbolize the authority to open and shut the kingdom of heaven. This authority is later extended to the other disciples (18:18). The words “bind” and “loose” were used by rabbis near the time of Christ to declare someone under a ban (“binding”) and relief of the ban (“loosing”). Sometimes this referred to expulsion or reinstatement at a synagogue. At other times binding and loosing indicated consignment to God’s judgment or acquittal from it. The “power of the keys” (or binding and loosing) of which Yeshua speaks is a spiritual authority like that he gave the disciples in John 20:23: “If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven; if you retain the sins of any, they are retained” (rsv).

The Pharisee party/Pharisees and scribes assumed that as teachers of the law they had power to shut the kingdom of heaven against others (Mt 23:13). Yet as blind guides they failed to recognize what Kefa had acknowledged—that Yeshua was the one in whom God’s kingdom had come. KIDRON

Valley and streambed running below the southeast wall of Yerushalem/Jerusalem and separating the city from the Mt of Olives on the east. It then turns southeast from Yerushalem and follows a winding course to the Dead Sea. The Kidron can be described as a torrent bed that is nearly always dry, since the watercourse flows only in the rainy season, partly maintained by the two irregular springs Gihon and Eyn-Rogel/En-rogel.

The Gihon was the vital water source for the old City of David, and in Hizkiyah’s/Hezekiah’s day an underground tunnel was cut in the rock to guarantee a water supply in time of siege, thus supplying the pool of Siloam within the city walls.

The term “brook” found in John 18:1 (kjv) would be better translated “winter flow” or “winter course,” since the original word intends to convey this seasonal character of the creek rather than to suggest a river.

The two most important functions of the Kidron Valley for the city of Yerushalem are military and funerary. The walls of the city have always towered over the valley, and its steepness made it extremely difficult for any attack to succeed from that side. Over the centuries rubble from nearby ruins has raised the floor of the valley. In places the present floor is some 40 feet (12.2 meters) above earlier historic levels; it is not certain how many ancient caves and tombs must lie below the present surface. The wide space just south of the city, where the Kidron meets and merges with the Tyropean and Hinom/Hinnom Valleys, has always been a favorite spot for the royal gardens, irrigated from the two nearby springs.

Since the fourth century AD, the Kidron has been called “the valley of Yehoshafat/Jehoshaphat” (Jl 3:12), scene of the judgment of nations at the last day, and this tradition is strong among both Muslims and Yehudim/Jews. Today the sides of the valley are crowded with tombs. Even before the exile it was a popular place for burial (2 Kgs 23:4-12 refers to the graves of the common people and to the dumping of idolatrous refuse there; see also 2 Chr 34:4-5).

The first reference to the Kidron Valley is in 2 Samuel 15:23, where the people and David crossed over toward the desert. This strategic move would give them a way of escape if rebellious Avshalom’s/Absalom’s forces decided to attack the city. The people and the king wept bitterly during this move (2 Sm 15:30) because it had such a depressing significance; David was abandoning Tsiyon/Zion without a fight. Later the offensive Shimei was forbidden to cross the Kidron by Shelomoh/Solomon (1 Kgs 2:36-38) on pain of death. Josephus mentions that the wicked queen Atalyah/Athaliah was put to death in the Kidron Valley (Antiquities 9.7.3), but it is not clear from 2 Kings 11:16 whether the horses’ entrance to the palace opened onto the Kidron.

The last reference to the Kidron is the occasion of Yeshua’s/Jesus’ crossing it with his disciples on the eve of his betrayal (Jn 18:1). The parallels with the crossing of David are interesting, considering the place David holds in the establishment of the biblical symbolism of king and kingdom. Eschatologically, Yirmiyah/Jeremiah foretells a time when the Kidron will be sacred to the Lord (Jer 31:38-40) as part of the restoration of Yisrael/Israel.

KINDNESS

The Bible is filled with illustrations of kindness. Yosef/Joseph wanted Par’oh’s/Pharaoh’s butler to show kindness by remembering him to Par’oh (Gn 40:14). Rahav/Rahab requested kind treatment from Yisrael/Israel for her protection of the two spies who had come into her home (Jos 2:12). Before he attacked Amalek, Sha’ul/Saul asked the Keynim/Kenites to leave the Amaleki/Amalekite territory, not wanting to kill them along with the Amalekim/Amalekites because of the kindness they had shown Yisrael when Yisrael came up from Mitsrayim/Egypt (1 Sm 15:6). David commended the men of Yavesh-Gilead/Jabesh-gilead for the kindness they had shown Sha’ul in giving his body a decent burial (2 Sm 2:5). Yonatan/Jonathan requested “unfailing kindness” of David so that he would not be killed (1 Sm 20:14-15). David extended this kindness to Yonatan’s son by granting him the right to eat at the king’s table (2 Sm 9:1-7).

It is the worst kind of ingratitude to return evil for kindness. Avimelek/Abimelech wanted Avraham/Abraham to swear that he would return kindness for kindness to his offspring (Gn 21:23). Avner/Abner showed kindness to Ish-Boshet/Ishbosheth by not delivering him over to David, while Ish-Boshet, in return, charged Avner with guilt regarding Sha’ul’s concubine, Ritspah/Rizpah (2 Sm 3:8). Hanun received David’s kind act of sending condolences on his father’s death by humiliating David’s messengers, thereby bringing on war between the two nations (10:2-19). Avshalom/Absalom rebuked Hushay/Hushai, David’s friend, for supposedly leaving David’s side when he needed him. Avshalom asked Hushay if that was the way he was repaying David’s friendship (2 Sm 16:17; see also 2 Chr 24:22).

God’s actions provide the outstanding illustrations of kindness in the Bible. The Levites praised God because he had proved to be a God of forgiveness, graciousness, compassion, and abundant lovingkindness (Neh 9:17-31). To highlight God’s virtue even more, they declared his kindness against the backdrop of Yisrael’s unfaithfulness. God did not forsake his people, even though they forsook him for a golden calf. He gave them his Spirit to instruct them. He gave them manna to eat and water to drink for 40 years in the wilderness. He gave them Kena’an/Canaan, a land in which to dwell.

The high point of God’s kindness was his provision of salvation for sinners, not on the basis of their works but on the basis of his mercy (Ti 3:4; see also Eph 2:7). Because of God’s great kindness toward them, in giving both physical and spiritual blessings, Christians are exhorted, as God’s elect, to put on hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience; that is, to show kindness to others in return for God’s kindness (Col 3:12). KING

The word melek (king) occurs more than 2,000 times in the Hebrew OT. It may refer to God (Ps 95:3) or to human rulers. Generally it designates one invested with ultimate authority and power over his subjects. In the OT, the word melek designates the ruler of a tribe (“the kings of Midyan/Midian,” Nm 31:8), a city (Yeriho/Jericho, Ay/Ai; cf. Jos 12:9-24, where 31 kings of city-states conquered by the Israelis/Israelites are listed), a nation (Yisrael/Israel, Yehudah/Judah, Amon/Ammon, Moav/Moab, Aram), or an international power (such as Mitsrayim/Egypt, Ashur/Assyria, Bavel/Babylonia, or Paras/Persia). Other words may also refer to royalty. The Pelishtim/Philistines introduced the title seren (lord) into Hebrew vocabulary. The five Pelishti/Philistine cities were ruled by five lords. Another word for an Israeli/Israelite king is nagid (ruler). Both Sha’ul/Saul and David were anointed as nagid over Yisrael (1 Sm 10:1; 16:13). In the NT and the Septuagint, the Greek version of the OT, the Greek word basileus has a meaning similar to the Hebrew melek. The NT basileus refers to secular rulers living in the first century, kings of Yisrael, rulers of the past, and the divine King, Yeshua/Jesus Christ.

The phrase “King of kings,” attributed to Yeshua (1 Tm 6:15), is a Hebrew expression meaning supreme or greatest king. For example, in Yehezkel’s/Ezekiel’s prediction of the fall of Tsor/Tyre, Nevukadnetsar/Nebuchadnezzar is named the “king of kings” (Ez 26:7). The great rulers of Ashur and Bavel introduced this title. Before their time, rulers were called either “king” or “great king,” as in 2 Kings 18:28: “Hear the word of the great king, the king of Ashur” (rsv). Later rulers had their titles adjusted to keep up with the expanse of their empires.
Kingship in Yisrael

God chose Avraham/Abraham as the father of nations; through him and his descendants the messianic rule would be established on earth. In his promises to Avraham, God repeatedly assured him that he would become the father of a mighty nation, to whom God would give the land of Kena’an/Canaan, and that kings would arise from his descendants (Gn 17:6). Avraham showed his acceptance of the rule of God over his family by obeying God’s command to be circumcised, which set the clan of Avraham apart for the service of God (vv 10-14). The ultimate purpose of God’s relation with Avraham and his descendants was that God would be King over Yisrael and that his people would show their acceptance of his rule by their faithful obedience to him (v 9).

At the heart of the covenant was God’s expectation of loyalty to his rule. Avraham and his descendants were to exercise their God-given “rule” over the nations by living in fellowship with the great King. Thus the Lord reestablished his dominion over mankind. Through Avraham and his descendants, he would raise up a “royal nation” to whom the full privileges of rule over his creation would be restored.

The Lord also made a covenant with Yisrael. This covenant was a sovereign administration of grace and promise by which the Lord consecrated the people unto himself by the sanctions of divine law and by his very presence. The nation, witnessing God’s care for them, had to learn that by their obedience to God’s expectations the theocratic kingdom might become a reality on earth. In the Sinaitic covenant the theocracy (the rule of God) was established. Yisrael was entrusted with the commandments, so that they might show themselves to be a theocratic nation, as God revealed to Mosheh/Moses: “Now if you will obey me and keep my covenant, you will be my own special treasure from among all the nations of the earth; for all the earth belongs to me. And you will be to me a kingdom of priests, my holy nation” (Ex 19:5-6, nlt). They were God’s elect for the sake of the nations; through Yisrael’s priestly obedience and intercession, the whole earth might know the Creator-Redeemer.

The qualities of God’s kingship were power, glory, fidelity, wisdom, concern, service, delegation of power to man, blessing and protection, just rule, judgment, vindication, and deliverance. Yisrael’s kingship was to be no different from God’s. Their varied and sometimes complex laws taught Yisrael to distinguish between what was holy and common, clean and unclean, the ways of God and the ways of the nations. The ways of God enhanced love, fidelity, justice, peace, harmony, service, concern for others, wise living, defense of the needy, and judgment of the guilty. The ways of the kingdoms of the world all too often promoted selfishness, anarchy, despotism, and disregard for justice.

The Lord also instituted an organizational structure designed to promote his theocratic purposes. In the wilderness Mosheh and the chosen leaders of Yisrael (Ex 18:19-26; Nm 11:24-25; cf. Dt 1:15-18) were God’s instruments for upholding his kingship in Yisrael. Upon Mosheh’s death, Yehoshua/Joshua took over the theocratic rule. The Lord was with him as he had been with Mosheh, and all Yisrael recognized the continuity of God’s rule in Yehoshua’s leadership (Dt 34:9; Jos 3:7; 4:14). Like Mosheh had before his death, Yehoshua charged the leadership and Yisrael to persevere in the gracious covenant relationship (Jos 23–24). However, Yisrael perished because of its greed, immorality, strife, and idolatry. During the period of the judges, each one did what was right in his own eyes (Jgs 17:6; 18:1; 19:1; 21:25). There was no king in the land in those days. The judges were military leaders whom the Lord raised up to deliver his people from their foreign oppressors. But God remained King, regardless of the fact that Yisrael lived as if he were not. The period of the judges demonstrated that apostate Yisrael, disobedient to their King, was unsuccessful in dealing with the surrounding nations.

The theocratic leadership was restored to Yisrael by the ministry of Shmuel/Samuel. He was born into a Levitical family and served the Lord at the Shiloh tabernacle. He was called to be a prophet—an office which had not been filled since Mosheh’s death (1 Sm 3:20-21). He was recognized as a judge in Yisrael (7:15). In Shmuel the offices of priest, prophet, and king were combined. He is never called king, as his lifestyle was that of a prophet rather than that of a ruler. The carefully calculated request of the people for a king was a rejection of Shmuel’s ministry. The people were not satisfied with the spiritual, charismatic leadership of Shmuel. In their search for a more dynamic leader they found in the kings of the surrounding nations attractive elements: power, manifestation of glory, and stability. Thus far the tribes had experienced several civil wars that endangered the unity of Yisrael. It was thought that a king would remedy all of the social and political problems. Though God had foreseen the days of the monarchy in the law (Dt 17:14-20), the people were motivated to introduce the kingship for secular rather than religious reasons: “Give us a king like all the other nations have” (1 Sm 8:5); “We want to be like the nations around us. Our king will govern us and lead us into battle” (v 20, nlt). Shmuel never accepted the idea of kingship; it was foreign to the theocratic ideal.

The crucial difference between kingship in Yisrael and kingship in neighboring lands lay in the fact that God endowed the king of Yisrael with his Spirit to establish his rule on earth. God ruled for his people, and his people benefited was from his rule; he was their provider, protector, and divine warrior.

Shmuel was instrumental in anointing Sha’ul (a sad example of kingship) and David (a good example of kingly rule under God). Sha’ul’s kingship revealed a despotic, uncaring attitude and self-aggrandizement. He was intent on establishing his dynasty, while not caring sufficiently for the people of God. Therefore, the Lord rejected his kingship (1 Sm 15:23).

David’s kingship, in contrast to Sha’ul’s/Saul’s, was in line with God’s because it reflected the glory of Yahweh’s kingship. David’s life and rule are taken up in the two books of Shmuel as a commentary on the pros and cons of kingship. Positively, David was a man after God’s heart, who sought the will of God, repented of his sin, and sought the glory of God. Negatively, David failed in his personal and family life to uphold the high standards of God’s law. Yet God was pleased to choose David’s dynasty as the lineage through which Yeshua/Jesus Christ would come. The prophet Natan/Nathan assured David that his dynasty would last: “Your dynasty and your kingdom will continue for all time before me, and your throne will be secure forever” (2 Sm 7:16, nlt). But God did not promise that it would be immune from prosecution or banishment.

The outstanding qualities of the kingship of David and his son Shelomoh/Solomon reflect the true theocratic intention: concern for the Lord, for a heart of wisdom and integrity, and for the well-being of God’s people. Concern for the Lord found expression in the preparation for and actual building of the temple (cf. Ps 132). Concern for integrity and wisdom is clearly evident, especially in David’s response to Natan’s rebuke (2 Sm 12) and in Shelomoh’s request to have a heart of wisdom (1 Kgs 3). Concern for the people comes to expression in their securing the borders against enemies, achieving national unification, and bringing opportunity for economic growth. The era of David and Shelomoh represented a true reflection of God’s kingship on earth.

The accounts in Kings and Chronicles unfold the subsequent history of kingship in Yisrael/Israel and Yehudah/Judah. The good kings followed the examples provided by David and Shelomoh in securing Yerushalem/Jerusalem against foreign invaders, in supplying for the needs of the temple, in having God’s people instructed in the word of God, and in modeling their rule after the law of Mosheh. A good Davidic king loved the Lord, the temple, the law, and God’s people. He served them as a good shepherd. Evil kings were those who rejected this model of kingship in favor of the pagan models. So Omri and Ahav/Ahab introduced the Phoenician culture with its Baalism, utterly disregarding the heritage of Yisrael.

The Davidic king was treated as a member of God’s household, being a “son” of the great King (cf. 2 Sm 7:14-16; Ps 2:6-7). The Davidic king was to be loyal to the great King, Yahweh. He, like Mosheh and Yehoshua, received his orders directly from the Lord; but unlike with Mosheh, the word of the Lord was mediated through the prophets. He, like Mosheh and Yehoshua, was expected to serve his God and his people.
The Messiah-King

The descendants of David failed to maintain and expand the theocracy. By the eighth and seventh centuries BC, it was apparent that even the greatest kings were dwarfed by the stature of David and Shelomoh. The prophets (Is 9:2-7; 11:1-9; Jer 33:14-16; Ez 34:22-31; Mi 5:2-5) spoke of another king, the Messiah, a descendant of David who would rule permanently and by whose rule the reign of God would extend to the ends of the earth. He would put down all opposition to God’s rule, remove all enemies, and bring in an era of universal peace and righteousness. The Messiah-King would reveal the perfections of divine rule, as the Spirit of God would be upon him. His kingship would be marked by service to the people of God, so that they would be a well-cared-for flock; he would serve them as their shepherd.

In the coming of Yeshua the messianic kingdom is more clearly revealed. He is the King of whom the angels said, “The Savior—yes, the Messiah, the Lord—has been born tonight in Beyt-Lehem/Bethlehem, the city of David!” (Lk 2:11, nlt). These magnificent words show continuity with the prophetic word. Yeshua is the Savior, whose role includes deliverance from sin but also deliverance from all causes of adversity, evil, and the effects of the curse. His mission pertains to both forgiveness and to the establishment of peace on earth (1:77-79). In this light we must look at Yeshua’s ministry of healing, feeding, opposing the forces of evil, suffering, and teaching as the establishment of God’s kingdom on earth. He is the King who serves, fights against the demonic powers, and overcomes. The resurrection marks his victory, and he is crowned with glory by being seated at the right hand of the Father (Acts 2:33-36; cf. 1 Cor 15:25). In being the Savior he is none other than Christ the Lord. The early apostolic preaching proclaimed that Yeshua is the Messiah of God and the Lord. The lordship of Yeshua is corollary to his being the Messiah. To those who call on him, he is the Savior-Messiah-Lord (Rom 10:9-15), but to those who reject him, he is the divine warrior, before whom all knees will bow and who will bring in the era of the Father’s judgment (cf. Rv 1:12-16; 19:11-21).

Yeshua taught his disciples that at his coming in glory he would be seated on his throne and all mankind would pay him obeisance. The enemies of God will be cast out from his presence, and the people of God will fully inherit the kingdom (Mt 25:31-46). In accordance with Yeshua’s teaching, the members of his body, the church, are expected to work out the theocratic ideal in their lives, that by their works and faith they may glorify the Father and show that they are his (Jn 17:20-26; cf. Mt 25:33-40). This is the biblical manner of witness that Yisrael failed to give and that the church is privileged to give; as Paulos/Paul wrote to Timotheos/Timothy:

I command you before God, who gives life to all, and before Christ Yeshua, . . . that you obey his commands with all purity. Then no one can find fault with you from now until our Lord Yeshua Christ returns. For at the right time Christ will be revealed from heaven by the blessed and only almighty God, the King of kings and Lord of lords. He alone can never die, and he lives in light so brilliant that no human can approach him. No one has ever seen him, nor ever will. To him be honor and power forever. Amen. (1 Tm 6:13-16, nlt)

Then Paulos gives several instructions as to how the people of God must demonstrate their allegiance to Yeshua. Throughout the book of Revelation, Yeshua is viewed as King over the church (Rv 4:2, 9-11; 5:1, 9-13). At his return his kingship will be established. At this time, the enemies of the cross will see the one whom they have rejected and will bow before the messianic King (1 Cor 15:25-28). “After that the end will come, when he [Yeshua] will turn the Kingdom over to God the Father, having put down all enemies of every kind” (v 24, nlt).
See also Israel, History of; Kingdom of God, Kingdom of Heaven.
